## What this notebook makes

One self-contained web page, `figures/migration_map.html`, that animates the
spring season:

- **Moving lines:** the simulated BirdFlow routes from notebook 03, one line
  per simulated bird, coloured by species, each with a fading tail.
- **Circles over Southern California:** the three radars from notebook 05,
  growing and shrinking with the birds detected aloft each night.
- **A control panel:** play/pause, a date slider, a radar chart with a
  "tonight" marker, species on/off switches, and a filter for routes that
  pass through our study states.
- **A Lights Out panel** (from notebook 06's results): whether tonight falls
  in the Lights Out San Diego program, whether it was one of the season's
  busiest nights, and whether it was overcast (when birds fly lower). The
  radar chart shades the program's peak weeks and marks the busiest nights.

The page is plain HTML and JavaScript, so it works on GitHub Pages: copy the
file into the website repository and link to it (see the end of this
notebook). It uses **deck.gl**, a free, open-source mapping library, which the
page loads from a public CDN when someone opens it.

**How it's built:** the page's design and behaviour live in
`templates/migration_map_template.html` (commented, so it can be edited). This
notebook only prepares the data and inserts it into that template. To change
how the page looks, edit the template and re-run this notebook.

**Data rules:** the page contains only *derived* data (simulated routes,
nightly radar totals, outlines), never raw eBird rasters, consistent with the
eBird Status & Trends terms (Educational use). The required citation and
disclaimer are printed at the bottom of the page.

```{r setup}
source(here::here("R", "config.R"))
source(here::here("R", "study_area.R"))

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
library(sf)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)

SEASON_START <- as.Date("2026-03-01")     # radar season, same as notebooks 05–06
SEASON_END   <- as.Date("2026-06-15")
RADAR_OUT    <- file.path(PATHS$derived, "radar", SEASON_LABEL)
SITE_DIR     <- PATHS$figures   # the map page sits with the other figures

# Species colours: the dark-surface version of our palette (the map uses a
# night theme). Fixed order; validated for colour-blind separation and for
# contrast against the map's land and water. The legend shows each species'
# name next to its colour, so identity never depends on colour alone.
SPECIES_COLS <- c("#3987e5", "#d95926", "#199e70", "#c98500", "#d55181", "#0ca30c")

# Species that migrate by DAY (tagged "day" in the legend: the night-time
# radar doesn't count them).
DAY_MIGRANTS <- c("rufhum")
```

## Step 1 · Load the simulated routes

```{r load-routes}
selection <- read_csv(file.path(PATHS$derived, "species_selection.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(selected, use == "routes + abundance") |>
  arrange(match(species_code, CANDIDATE_SPECIES))

route_file <- \(code) file.path(PATHS$routes, paste0(code, "_", SEASON_LABEL, "_routes.geojson"))

# Keep only species whose route file exists (notebook 03 must have run).
selection <- selection |> filter(file.exists(route_file(species_code)))
stopifnot("No route files found: run notebook 03 first" = nrow(selection) > 0)

points <- map_dfr(selection$species_code, \(code) {
  g  <- st_read(route_file(code), quiet = TRUE)
  xy <- st_coordinates(g)
  st_drop_geometry(g) |>
    mutate(species_code = code, lon = xy[, 1], lat = xy[, 2])
})

points |> count(species_code, name = "route_points")
```

## Step 2 · Turn route points into animation paths

The animation needs, for every simulated bird, its positions in order and the
**day of year** it is at each one.

One detail matters for how the animation looks. BirdFlow routes include
**stopovers**, where a bird stays in the same place for one or more weeks
(`stay_len`). If we only gave the map the day a bird *arrived* at a stopover,
the map would slide it slowly towards the next stop the whole time it was
resting. So for each stopover we add a second point at the day the bird
*leaves*, at the same position. The bird then waits, then flies.

This works whichever way the route file stores stopovers (one row per week,
or one row per stop with its length), because we combine consecutive rows at
the same position and take the later of the two possible leaving dates.

```{r build-trips}
trips_long <- points |>
  mutate(date     = as.Date(date),
         stay_len = coalesce(as.numeric(stay_len), 1)) |>
  arrange(species_code, route_id, date) |>
  group_by(species_code, route_id) |>
  # A new "run" starts whenever the position changes.
  mutate(run = cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(lon) != 0 | diff(lat) != 0))) |>
  group_by(species_code, route_id, crosses_study_area, run) |>
  summarise(lon    = first(lon), lat = first(lat),
            arrive = min(date),
            leave  = max(max(date), min(date) + 7 * (first(stay_len) - 1)),
            .groups = "drop_last") |>
  # Never leave after arriving at the next stop.
  mutate(leave = pmin(leave, lead(arrive, default = as.Date("2100-01-01")))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_longer(c(arrive, leave), values_to = "date") |>
  distinct(species_code, route_id, crosses_study_area, lon, lat, date) |>
  arrange(species_code, route_id, date) |>
  # BirdFlow dates describe a typical year; we use day of year for the
  # animation (a leap year would shift dates by at most one day).
  mutate(doy = yday(date))

# One record per simulated bird. Coordinates are rounded to 0.01° (~1 km),
# far finer than BirdFlow's ~100 km cells, to keep the page small.
trips <- trips_long |>
  group_by(species_code, route_id, crosses_study_area) |>
  filter(n() >= 2) |>                       # need at least two points to move
  summarise(p = list(unname(round(cbind(lon, lat), 2))),
            t = list(doy), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(s = match(species_code, selection$species_code) - 1,   # 0-based index for JavaScript
         x = as.integer(crosses_study_area))

trips |> count(species_code, name = "simulated_birds")
```

## Step 3 · Species summary for the legend

```{r species}
species_json <- trips |>
  group_by(species_code) |>
  summarise(n_routes = n(), pct_study = round(100 * mean(x))) |>
  right_join(selection |> select(species_code, common_name), by = "species_code") |>
  arrange(match(species_code, selection$species_code)) |>
  mutate(color = map(seq_along(species_code), \(i) as.vector(col2rgb(SPECIES_COLS[i]))))

species_json |> select(common_name, n_routes, pct_study)
```

## Step 4 · Radar: one value per station per night

```{r radar}
radar <- list.files(file.path(RADAR_OUT, "nights"), pattern = "\\.csv$",
                    full.names = TRUE) |>
  map_dfr(\(f) read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE,
                        col_types = cols(night = col_date(),
                                         peak_time_local = col_character()))) |>
  filter(status == "ok", night >= SEASON_START, night <= SEASON_END) |>
  mutate(doy = yday(night))

# Station coordinates, read from a saved radar profile (as in notebook 06).
coords <- map_dfr(RADAR_STATIONS, \(s) {
  f <- list.files(file.path(RADAR_OUT, "profiles"), pattern = paste0("^", s, "_"),
                  full.names = TRUE)[1]
  v <- readRDS(f)
  tibble(code = s, lat = v$attributes$where$lat, lon = v$attributes$where$lon)
})

# Display names, and where each label sits relative to its circle (pixels).
# The three radars are close together, so labels point in different
# directions to avoid overlapping.
station_info <- tibble(
  code   = c("KNKX", "KSOX", "KVTX"),
  label  = c("San Diego", "Santa Ana Mountains", "Los Angeles (Ventura)"),
  offset = list(c(-12, 6), c(12, 0), c(-12, -6))   # [right, down] in pixels
)

doy_range <- yday(SEASON_START):yday(SEASON_END)

# One array per station: birds/km for each night (NA where missing).
pass <- map(RADAR_STATIONS, \(s) {
  r <- radar |> filter(station == s)
  unname(r$total_passage[match(doy_range, r$doy)])
})

stations_json <- coords |>
  left_join(station_info, by = "code") |>
  mutate(offset = map(offset, unname))

stations_json
```

## Step 4b · Lights Out context (from notebook 06)

Notebook 06 found that the busiest nights carry much of the season and that
birds fly lower on overcast nights. Here we tag each night so the map can
show it. Everything comes from files notebook 06 already saved; if 06 hasn't
been run, the panel simply shows the program dates.

```{r lights-out}
PROGRAM_SEASON <- as.Date(c("2026-03-01", "2026-06-15"))   # Lights Out San Diego, spring
PROGRAM_PEAK   <- as.Date(c("2026-04-15", "2026-05-15"))   # its "critical peak"
N_BUSIEST      <- 10      # "busiest nights" = top 10 by the three radars' mean
OVERCAST_PCT   <- 80      # cloud cover above this counts as overcast (as in 06)

# Busiest nights: mean of the three radars, top N.
busy_doy <- radar |>
  group_by(doy) |>
  summarise(mean_pass = mean(total_passage), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(mean_pass, n = N_BUSIEST) |>
  pull(doy)

# Overcast nights at San Diego (KNKX), from 06's nightly weather.
weather_file <- file.path(PATHS$derived, "weather",
                          paste0("nightly_features_", SEASON_LABEL, ".csv"))
overcast_doy <- if (file.exists(weather_file)) {
  read_csv(weather_file, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    filter(station == "KNKX", cloud > OVERCAST_PCT) |>
    pull(night) |> yday()
} else integer(0)

# Share of San Diego's birds that fly before 11 pm (06, "lights_out_hours").
hours_file <- file.path(PATHS$derived, "lights_out_hours.csv")
before_11 <- if (file.exists(hours_file)) {
  h <- read_csv(hours_file, show_col_types = FALSE) |> filter(station == "KNKX", start == 23)
  if (nrow(h) == 1) round(100 * (1 - h$covered)) else NA
} else NA

lights_json <- list(
  season = yday(PROGRAM_SEASON), peak = yday(PROGRAM_PEAK),
  busy = sort(busy_doy), overcast = sort(overcast_doy),
  n_busiest = N_BUSIEST, before_11_pct = before_11
)
str(lights_json)
```

## Step 5 · Background map

Land outlines for North and Central America, plus our study states outlined
on top. Both come from the `maps` package (no downloads), simplified so the
page stays small.

```{r basemap}
sf_use_s2(FALSE)   # planar geometry is fine for simplifying outlines

americas <- c("USA", "Canada", "Mexico", "Guatemala", "Belize", "Honduras",
              "El Salvador", "Nicaragua", "Costa Rica", "Panama", "Cuba",
              "Jamaica", "Haiti", "Dominican Republic", "Bahamas",
              "Colombia", "Venezuela")

land <- maps::map("world", regions = americas, plot = FALSE, fill = TRUE) |>
  st_as_sf()
land <- suppressWarnings(st_set_crs(land, 4326)) |>   # datum note: see R/study_area.R
  st_make_valid()
# Simplify to ~0.05° (~5 km). sf warns that this tolerance is in degrees for
# lon/lat data; that's what we intend, so the warning is silenced.
land <- suppressWarnings(st_simplify(land, dTolerance = 0.05, preserveTopology = TRUE))

study <- study_states(merge = TRUE) |> st_transform(4326)

sf_use_s2(TRUE)

#' sf object -> GeoJSON text, coordinates rounded to 2 decimals (~1 km).
as_geojson <- function(x) {
  f <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  st_write(st_geometry(x), f, driver = "GeoJSON", quiet = TRUE,
           layer_options = "COORDINATE_PRECISION=2")
  paste(readLines(f, warn = FALSE), collapse = "")
}
land_json  <- as_geojson(land)
study_json <- as_geojson(study)

c(land_kb = nchar(land_json) %/% 1000, study_kb = nchar(study_json) %/% 1000)
```

## Step 6 · Assemble the page

```{r assemble}
# Animation runs from the earliest route or radar night to the latest.
time_start <- min(map_dbl(trips$t, min), min(doy_range))
time_end   <- min(max(map_dbl(trips$t, max), max(doy_range)), yday(SEASON_END) + 14)

html_escape <- \(x) x |> gsub("&", "&amp;", x = _, fixed = TRUE) |>
  gsub("<", "&lt;", x = _, fixed = TRUE) |> gsub(">", "&gt;", x = _, fixed = TRUE)

credits <- c(
  "Lines are <strong>simulated</strong> routes from BirdFlow models of each species, not tracked birds. Radar counts are birds per km of migration front per night, estimated with vol2bird.",
  html_escape(paste("Routes:", "Fuentes, M., Van Doren, B. M., Fink, D., & Sheldon, D. (2023). BirdFlow: Learning seasonal bird movements from eBird data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 14(3), 923–938. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14052")),
  html_escape(paste("eBird data:", EBIRD_CITATION)),
  html_escape(EBIRD_DISCLAIMER),
  html_escape("Radar: NOAA National Weather Service Radar Operations Center (1991). NEXRAD Level II Base Data. NOAA NCEI. doi:10.7289/V5W9574V. Processed with vol2bird / bioRad (Dokter et al. 2011)."),
  html_escape("Lights Out San Diego: San Diego Bird Alliance (program dates for spring 2026). Busiest nights, cloud cover and the share of birds flying before 11 pm come from our radar and weather analysis (notebook 06; weather: Open-Meteo / ERA5, CC BY 4.0)."),
  html_escape("Map library: deck.gl (MIT licence). Outlines: R maps package.")
)

map_data <- list(
  species = species_json |>
    transmute(code = species_code, name = common_name, color, n_routes, pct_study,
              diurnal = species_code %in% DAY_MIGRANTS),
  trips   = trips |> select(s, x, p, t),
  radar   = list(stations = stations_json |> select(code, label, lon, lat, offset),
                 doy0 = min(doy_range), pass = pass),
  lights  = lights_json,
  time    = list(start = time_start, end = time_end, year = year(SEASON_START)),
  # Initial view: the Pacific Flyway from Mexico to British Columbia.
  view    = list(longitude = -116, latitude = 36, zoom = 3.4, pitch = 0, bearing = 0),
  credits = credits
)

json <- toJSON(map_data, auto_unbox = TRUE, na = "null", digits = NA)
# Insert the GeoJSON outlines as raw JSON (they're already JSON text).
json <- sub("^\\{", paste0('{"land":', land_json, ',"study":', study_json, ','), json)
# Safety: text inside a <script> block must never contain "</".
json <- gsub("</", "<\\/", json, fixed = TRUE)

template <- paste(readLines(here::here("templates", "migration_map_template.html"),
                            warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), collapse = "\n")
# Splice the data in at the placeholder. (Split-and-paste rather than sub(),
# because sub() would treat backslashes in the data as special characters.)
parts <- strsplit(template, "__MAP_DATA__", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
stopifnot("Template must contain the data placeholder exactly once" = length(parts) == 2)
page <- paste0(parts[1], json, parts[2])

out <- file.path(SITE_DIR, "migration_map.html")
# Write as UTF-8 explicitly so characters like "–" and "×" survive on any
# computer, whatever its language settings.
con <- file(out, open = "w", encoding = "UTF-8")
writeLines(enc2utf8(page), con)
close(con)
cat("Wrote", out, "-", round(file.size(out) / 1e6, 2), "MB\n")
```

## Step 7 · Look at it, then publish

**Preview:** open `figures/migration_map.html` in a web browser (in RStudio's
Files pane: click it → *View in Web Browser*). It needs an internet connection
the first time, to load the deck.gl library.

Check:

- routes start in Mexico/Central America and move north through the season;
- the radar circles swell in late April, matching notebook 06's timing;
- hovering a moving dot shows its species; hovering a radar circle shows that
  night's count;
- the species switches and the "only routes through the study states" filter
  work;
- the radar chart's shaded band covers April 15 – May 15, and moving the
  slider onto one of its dotted nights shows "One of the season's 10
  busiest nights" in the Lights Out panel.

**Publish on the website (GitHub Pages):**

1. Copy `figures/migration_map.html` into the website repository (for example as
   `map.html`, or into a `map/` folder as `index.html`).
2. Commit and push. GitHub Pages serves it at
   `https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/map.html`.
3. Link to it from the site's pages, or embed it in an existing page:

   ```html
   <iframe src="map.html" title="Spring migration map" width="100%" height="900"
           style="border:0"></iframe>
   ```

**When data change** (a different species, the fall season, more routes),
re-run notebooks 03 and 07 and copy the new file over. The template doesn't
change.

## Limitations to state alongside the map

- **Routes are simulated.** Each line is a draw from a probability model of the
  species' movement, not a tracked individual. The *pattern* across 200 lines
  per species is the result; any single line is illustrative.
- **Timing comes from a typical year** (eBird's modelled weeks), while the
  radar circles show **spring 2026** nights. The match between them is the
  subject of notebook 06, not something the map proves.
- **Weekly steps.** BirdFlow moves birds once a week, so the animation
  interpolates smoothly between weekly positions; real birds fly in nightly
  hops with rest days in between.
